findings.summary: A birth–death process is a continuous-time Markov process modeling population size changes through only two transition types: births that increment the count and deaths that decrement it. Introduced by William Feller, it uses positive birth rates {λ_i} and death rates {μ_i} to define transitions between integer states. The process evolves according to small-time probabilities where a birth occurs with probability λ_iΔt+o(Δt), a death with μ_iΔt+o(Δt), and no change with 1−(λ_i+μ_i)Δt+o(Δt). Its behavior—recurrence, transience, or ergodicity—is determined by the ratios of these rates, and when ergodic, a stationary distribution π_k exists, calculated from the product of rate ratios. The model underlies applications in demography, queueing theory, epidemiology, and phylodynamics, where it tracks infection spread or population evolution over time.

mechanisms.title: State transition dynamics
mechanisms.explanation: At each state i, the process moves to i+1 (birth) with rate λ_i or to i−1 (death) with rate μ_i. Over a small interval Δt, the probability of a birth is λ_iΔt+o(Δt), of a death is μ_iΔt+o(Δt), and of no change is 1−(λ_i+μ_i)Δt+o(Δt). Transitions involving multiple births or deaths are negligible (higher-order o(Δt)). This defines the infinitesimal generator of the continuous-time Markov chain.

mechanisms.title: Recurrence and ergodicity criteria
mechanisms.explanation: The process is recurrent if the infinite sum of product ratios ∏(μ_n/λ_n) diverges; it is ergodic if that sum diverges while the sum of product ratios ∏(λ_{n−1}/μ_n) converges; it is null-recurrent if both sums diverge. These conditions, established by Karlin and McGregor, classify long-term behavior without guaranteeing a stationary distribution in the null-recurrent case.

unknowns: Exact functional forms of λ_i and μ_i for specific real-world populations

How finite-server constraints modify the infinite-population assumptions
